title: From column to surface: connecting the performance in simulating aerosol optical properties and PM <sub>2.5</sub> concentrations in the NASA GEOSCCM
abstract: Abstract. Aerosols are a key climate forcer and harmful to human health at the surface. Accurately modeling aerosol optical properties, mass loading and their relationship is important for constraining aerosol-climate forcing and characterizing particulate matter pollution exposure. We investigate the drivers of uncertainties in the NASA Goddard Earth Observing System Chemistry Climate Model (GEOSCCM) in simulating aerosols by focusing on the link between aerosol optical properties and mass. We compare a GEOSCCM hindcast with long-term coincident observations including satellite AOD measurements, speciated PM2.5 datasets from observations-model data fusion, and ground-based measurements of aerosol mass and optical properties. We analyze regional trends and seasonal variations of AOD and PM2.5, and surface aerosol properties, including relative humidity's role in hygroscopic enhancement. This work also presents the first extensive assessment of GEOSCCM's aerosol component with observational data. Our findings show that biases in PM2.5 components and relative humidity significantly impact simulated aerosol scattering at the surface, while scattering efficiency assumptions align with observations. This indicates that errors in simulated scattering relate more to simulated aerosol speciated mass and relative humidity than optical properties and size distribution assumptions in GEOSCCM. Our work highlights the importance of relative humidity biases on aerosol scattering enhancement for climate models where meteorology is not prescribed. Findings suggest improvements in GEOSCCM aerosols mass and optical properties could be achieved through updating emission inventories, especially over biomass burning regions, reducing nitrate biases, and improving relative humidity simulation.
problem: Climate models show significant uncertainties in simulating aerosols because errors in modeled PM2.5 composition and relative humidity create a disconnect between aerosol optical properties (like AOD) and surface mass, impacting both climate forcing and pollution exposure characterization.
method: This study proposes an assessment approach that compares a GEOSCCM hindcast with coincident satellite and ground-based observations of aerosol optical properties and mass to investigate and identify the drivers of uncertainties in the model's aerosol simulations.
task: The task is to investigate drivers of uncertainty in the NASA GEOSCCM's aerosol simulations by assessing the modeled link between aerosol optical properties and surface PM2.5 mass against observational data.
innovation: This paper presents the first extensive assessment of the NASA GEOSCCM's aerosol component, identifying that uncertainties in simulated aerosol scattering are driven primarily by biases in PM2.5 composition and relative humidity rather than by the model's optical property assumptions.

GMI oxidants and nitric acid are one-way coupled to GOCART sulfate and nitrate algorithms. GOCART aerosol optical properties are pre-computed for each aerosol tracer and saved in look up tables (LUTs).
